chapter: The Dallas nightclub and Jesse Stone's band
title: Working for tips at a roadhouse in Dallas, Missouri
summary: The band takes a no-salary job outside Kansas City, pools tips in a kitty and visits Kansas City on weekends.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: So now you're up there at Saint Joseph, Missouri. When did you get into Kansas City?
Okay, now we're on our way. We got into Saint Joe, and as I said, we were sort of stranded there, and --
This is about 1928 now. We're up to 1928.

We're into '28. So now, we had to pull out of Saint Joe. Jesse Stone found a job for us, in a place called Dallas, Missouri, which is about 34 miles out of Kansas City. This was a beautiful, you might say almost like a roadhouse, only it was built in a nightclub style, but it's way outside.

That's right, you know. You might call it like a roadhouse. Only there was a lot of money spent there, and the guy says if we wanted to work we could work there for room and board and whatever tips we could make. We had no salary.

And so we accepted this. This was better than what we had. So we worked there, and we started to draw in people in there, and we made pretty good tips. We were well-organized, so none of the tips could we divide up. We all had to put them in the kitty, and the --
The kitty's the box that you put everything that --
Set it up on the piano, or someplace, where everybody can see it, and --
-- come and deposit this money in.
-- add to this money, like if they want to make a request, if they want to drop a dollar or fifty cents in it, or what not, they would do so.

And the man that owned the place had an old raggedy car outside that he'd let us use, and on weekends we used to drive into Kansas City to get our hair cut, and go around to the pool hall, and go around as many musicians as we could find, and go in, say hello, and whatnot, and it was a thrill. Kansas City was blooming then. They was full of jazz. They had all of these beautiful guys, and we would see like Benny Moten, you know, and --
